kid.question: What relationship does God promise His people?

options.text: They will be His people and He their God
They will be His builders and He their king
They will be His soldiers and He their captain
They will be His messengers and He their teacher

kid.explanation: God promises that they will dwell in the land given their fathers, be His people, and have Him as their God.

kid.question: What will God increase to end the people's famine?

options.text: Trade and silver from other nations
Grain and fruit from the land
Fish and salt from the sea
Bread and oil from the royal storehouse

kid.explanation: God will call for grain and multiply tree fruit and field produce so famine no longer brings reproach.

kid.question: What will the people remember after these promises?

options.text: Their skill at rebuilding the walls
Their victories over the neighboring nations
Their kindness toward the foreign kings
Their own wrong ways and deeds

kid.explanation: The people will remember their evil ways and feel shame over their iniquities and abominations.

kid.question: What will the once-ruined land be compared to?

options.text: The plains of Moab
The garden of Eden
The mountain of Sinai
The wilderness of Egypt

kid.explanation: The desolate land becomes tilled and is described as like the garden of Eden, with rebuilt, inhabited cities.

kid.question: What fills the valley where God takes Ezekiel?

options.text: Many very dry bones
Many empty water jars
Many fallen stone pillars
Many broken wooden carts

kid.explanation: In the spirit Ezekiel is placed in a valley full of very dry bones and led around them.

kid.question: How does Ezekiel answer when God asks if they can live?

options.text: Lord God, show me how
Lord God, tell me when
Lord God, send Your help
Lord God, You know

kid.explanation: Ezekiel responds, 'O Lord God, thou knowest,' placing the answer in God's knowledge.

kid.question: What happens as Ezekiel first speaks to the bones?

options.text: They stand and begin speaking
They crack and turn to dust
They shake and come together
They scatter across the open valley

kid.explanation: As he prophesies, there is a noise and shaking, and the bones come together bone to bone.

kid.question: After the first prophecy, what is still missing in Ezekiel 37:8?

options.text: Sinews joining the bones
Flesh upon the bones
Breath within the bodies
Skin covering the bodies

kid.explanation: Sinews, flesh, and skin form, but there is no breath until Ezekiel prophesies again as commanded.

kid.question: Whom do the bones represent?

options.text: The builders of the temple
The whole house of Israel
The armies of Babylon
The kings of surrounding nations

kid.explanation: God identifies the bones as Israel, whose people say their hope is lost and they are cut off.

kid.question: What does God tell Ezekiel to do with two sticks?

options.text: Write on them and join them
Carve them and plant them
Measure them and hide them
Break them and burn them

kid.explanation: He is to write for Judah and for Joseph on the sticks and join them into one in his hand.

high-school.question: How do material blessings relate to the people's memory of wrongdoing?

options.text: Abundance is accompanied by recognition and shame for their evil ways
Abundance is delayed until their former enemies admit causing every wrong
Abundance is presented as proof that their earlier choices were already righteous
Abundance is reserved for those who can forget the deeds of their ancestors

high-school.explanation: God promises land, cleansing, and food, then says they will remember and loathe their own evil ways; it is not for their merit.

high-school.question: What makes the renewed landscape a witness to surrounding nations?

options.text: Desolate fields remain untilled while foreign merchants pay for the restored temple
Desolate fields are divided among foreign nations who abandon their earlier idols
Ruined cities and desolate fields visibly display God's rebuilding and planting
Ruined cities remain empty while new armies demonstrate Israel's growing strength

high-school.explanation: The visible change to inhabited cities and a garden-like land leads nearby nations to know the Lord rebuilds and plants.

high-school.question: What image describes the renewed population of the cities?

options.text: Crowds like the soldiers at Babylon's city gates
Crowds like the workers at Assyria's royal quarries
Crowds like the merchants at Egypt's trading ports
Crowds like the holy flocks at Jerusalem's feasts

high-school.explanation: God compares the coming flocks of people in the waste cities with holy flocks at Jerusalem's solemn feasts.

high-school.question: Which detail is emphasized before God asks whether the bones can live?

options.text: They are separated from their owners' old weapons
They are arranged for a royal burial
They are very numerous and very dry
They are guarded by the captors' remaining soldiers

high-school.explanation: The valley contains very many, very dry bones before God asks whether they can live and Ezekiel defers to His knowledge.

high-school.question: What does the first act of prophesying accomplish?

options.text: Bones rise and leave the valley, but still lack a destination
Bones assemble and receive bodily form, but still lack breath
Bones move and defeat their enemies, but still lack a leader
Bones speak and name their families, but still lack their land

high-school.explanation: The first prophecy brings noise, shaking, joined bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, yet no breath.

high-school.question: What does Ezekiel see after the second prophecy in Ezekiel 37:9-10?

options.text: The bodies disappear and leave a newly planted valley
The bodies divide and form two separate nations again
The bodies speak and ask to be returned to their graves
The bodies live and stand as an exceedingly great army

high-school.explanation: Breath enters after the commanded prophecy, and they live and stand on their feet as a great army.

high-school.question: How does God interpret the vision for a hopeless Israel?

options.text: He promises life, opened graves, His spirit, and placement in their land
He promises influence among their captors and new authority in the foreign court
He promises a restored temple built by foreign kings and staffed by new priests
He promises separate homelands for each tribe under princes chosen by their elders

high-school.explanation: God identifies the bones as Israel and answers their lost hope with opened graves, His spirit, life, and return to their land.

high-school.question: What will lead the people to recognize the Lord in this promise?

options.text: He will require foreign kings to complete the prophecy first
He will perform the restoration He has spoken
He will explain the vision after appointing a new prophet
He will preserve the graves until the people rebuild the temple

high-school.explanation: They will know He is the Lord when He opens their graves and gives His spirit and land, having both spoken and performed.

high-school.question: Which pairing is assigned to the two written sticks?

options.text: Judah with companions, and Joseph associated with Ephraim
Judah with companions, and Levi associated with Aaron
Benjamin with companions, and Reuben associated with Simeon
Benjamin with companions, and Joseph associated with Manasseh

high-school.explanation: One is for Judah and companions; the other is for Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and companions of Israel.

high-school.question: How is the sign presented to the people?

options.text: A hidden action waits until a foreign ruler demands a written record
A visible action invites a question and receives God's explanation
A private dream requires the people to select which prophet should interpret it
A temple ceremony replaces explanation with a vote among the elders

high-school.explanation: The people ask what the sticks mean; Ezekiel gives God's words and holds the inscribed sticks before their eyes.

expert.question: What tension does the promised restoration maintain concerning Israel's worthiness?

options.text: Material abundance removes the need to acknowledge the ways that led to judgment
Renewed covenant life includes shame for past conduct rather than endorsement of it
Renewed covenant life depends on proving that earlier conduct had been falsely condemned
Material abundance transfers the moral blame from Israel to its former foreign captors

expert.explanation: God promises covenant belonging and provision while requiring remembrance and shame and repeating that He does not act for their sakes.

expert.question: What serves as public evidence for the concluding declaration in Ezekiel 36:36?

options.text: Cultivated fields and rebuilt cities reveal the Lord's work of planting and rebuilding
A new king renames the main city Eden to establish the borders of Israel
The cities' gardens display the royal builders' success in training the returning farmers
Ruins left as memorials display the continuing judgment while the fields remain unplanted

expert.explanation: The formerly desolate land becomes garden-like, and neighboring survivors recognize that the Lord builds and plants.

expert.question: What does the invitation to inquire add to the announced increase of people?

options.text: Promised divine action is held together with Israel's petitioning Him to do it
Promised divine action is withdrawn until the nations petition on Israel's behalf
Israel's petition replaces the earlier promise with a smaller population of shepherds
Israel's petition transfers responsibility for the rebuilding to Jerusalem's former priests

expert.explanation: Even after declaring He will act, God says He will be inquired of by Israel to do it for them, promising flocks of people.

expert.question: How does the opening dialogue establish the source of the bones' possible life?

options.text: Ezekiel defers to God's knowledge, and God announces the breath He will provide
Ezekiel rejects the possibility, and God asks him to select the least damaged bones
Ezekiel proposes a method, and God tells him to test it before speaking to the valley
Ezekiel claims prior knowledge, and God asks him to recruit physicians from the city

expert.explanation: Ezekiel says God knows; God then commands prophecy and promises breath, bodily restoration, and life.

expert.question: What distinction is dramatized by the vision's two stages?

options.text: The first prophecy restores the land; the second prophecy constructs the bodies from its soil
Bodily reassembly is complete life; the commanded breath merely supplies speech to the army
Bodily reassembly is not yet life; the commanded breath brings living standing bodies
The first prophecy restores Israel; the second prophecy replaces Israel with a foreign army

expert.explanation: After reassembly the bodies lack breath; a further prophecy to the breath is followed by their living and standing.

expert.question: How does the interpretation connect the breath scene with the promised restoration?

options.text: The joining of the bones corresponds to the division of land among tribes
Skin covering the bodies corresponds to the rebuilding of the sanctuary in Jerusalem
The army standing upright corresponds to Israel conquering the kingdoms surrounding its land
Breath entering the bodies corresponds to God's spirit bringing Israel renewed life

expert.explanation: Breath brings life in the scene; in its interpretation God promises His spirit, life, and settlement in their land.

expert.question: What does the explanation identify as the hopelessness being answered?

options.text: Israel's fear that its king has broken an alliance and cannot return
Israel's own claim to be dried up, without hope, and cut off
Israel's grief that the exiles have lost the law and cannot worship
Israel's complaint that its crops have failed because rainfall has stopped

expert.explanation: God explicitly connects the bones with the whole house of Israel and quotes their lost-hope language before promising opened graves and life.

expert.question: What actions accompany the placement in the land promised in Ezekiel 37:12-14?

options.text: Forgiving the foreign nations and bringing their rulers to Jerusalem for instruction
Restoring the former priesthood and appointing a new king over Babylon's remaining armies
Opening the people's ears and commissioning them to warn the surrounding foreign nations
Opening the people's graves and putting God's spirit within them

expert.explanation: The explanation combines opened graves, coming up, God's spirit, life, and placement in their land.

expert.question: What movement connects the physical action with the divine declaration about the sticks?

options.text: Two in God's hand become a command to erase the names already written by Ezekiel
One in Ezekiel's hand becomes a command to separate them between two foreign kings
One in Ezekiel's hand becomes a promise of one in God's hand
Two in God's hand become a promise of two permanently rival houses in Ezekiel's hand

expert.explanation: Ezekiel joins them into one in his hand; God's explanation declares He will make them one in His hand.

expert.question: What relationship between sign, question, and word is prescribed?

options.text: The people's question is postponed until the sticks are buried outside the settlement
The people's question receives a divine declaration while the written sticks remain visible
The written sticks are exchanged so the elders can decide which name should survive
The written sticks are removed so the people can supply an interpretation without words

expert.explanation: Their anticipated question is answered with 'Thus saith the Lord God,' and the sticks are held before their eyes.
